blocks.html: Staying current on AI/ML means drowning in hundreds of clickbait articles a day, which produces FOMO and impostor anxiety and eats time that should go to building. Existing news apps make this worse — they are engineered to always surface something, which is the exact incentive that feeds the anxiety.

Kill FOMO, don't feed it. Success is the fewest items you'd regret missing — not the most items covered. The system is explicitly allowed to say "quiet day, go build." Two jobs: (a) be aware and understand why it matters (conversational currency), and (b) get hands-on and understand tradeoffs (weekly homework grounded in your repos).
Five production agents on a pipeline, plus an eval/learning subsystem that measures the pipeline and adapts it to you over time.

blocks.html: Which LLM / agentic concept each agent uses, and for what. Built for the Framer today; the rest are the intended design. Agents are decoupled from each other via JSON contracts, and from their tools via MCP where a real boundary exists.

head: Agent
Concepts used
rows: MCP servers for source fetching (web / arXiv / GitHub) · source-reputation priors (Tier A–D) · deterministic ingestion (no LLM where a fetch suffices) · graded on recall

Verification harness for provenance / corroboration / dedup · classifier scored on precision + recall (recall-biased to avoid FOMO) · reputation priors for materiality · Suppressed-drawer audit log (false-negative eval)

Batched single structured call (frames all items at once) · structured output (JSON schema) · prompt caching on the reused system prompt · model routing (Opus frames, Haiku checks) · reflection loop for the faithfulness self-check · context injection from profile (no hardcoded facts) · prompt-as-file (verbatim markers) · cost circuit-breaker + usage ledger

MCP (GitHub server) for grounding homework in your repos · code-grounding assertions for verification · behavioral outcome signals (completion, actual time) · batched heavy run Fridays (model routing / cost) · streaming for long outputs

Longitudinal meta-eval (graded on slope over time) · credit assignment across the pipeline (delayed reward) · human-in-the-loop labels · two-tier action gating (auto vs human-gated) · anti-echo-chamber diversity guardrail · held-out set (train/test hygiene)

LLM intent-routing with deterministic fast-paths (don't LLM-route what a button can) · agent dispatch (URL → Scout, question → chat, feedback / "explore X" → Tuner) · response collation + guardrail checks · the one live-API agent in front of the otherwise-batch pipeline

Read-only sensor (Evaluator) · diagnosis → action with predicted-vs-actual accountability (Prescriber) · report + elicitation, where your answers become gold labels (Control Room) · regression gate on a golden set before shipping

blocks.html: Ordered input → process → output. Paths carry a plain description; where a file is a contract between agents, its shape is given.

head: Kind
Path — what it is
Status
rows:
config/profile.json
Who the reader is and what the rules are: role, interests, categories, plus doThisCategory and examplesOnlyForCategories. Injected at run time so nothing personal is hardcoded. Later written by the Tuner.

prompts/framer-prompt.md
The system prompt, verbatim and nothing else. This is the text sent to the model and the text that gets cached.

prompts/framer-contract.md
The I/O contract and hard rules. Documentation — never sent to the model.

data/verified/gatekeeper_<date>.json — the contract between two agents
Shape: date, items[] → id · category · headline · tags · source_excerpt · sources[]. No user_id: the verified pool is shared across readers. source_excerpt is the only text the Framer may draw facts from.

config/scout-sources.md
Scout’s Tier A–D seed source list with reputation priors.

agents/framer.py
Reads all of the above; makes two API calls (write, then grade); verifies quotes; enforces the profile rules in code; computes reading time and counts; writes the brief and appends its spend.

data/evals/run_evals.py
Regrades a frozen golden case with the current grader, asserts the structural rules, scores usefulness, and exits non-zero on any hard-gate failure.

data/briefs/framer_<date>.json — the Framer’s product
Shape: the verified item fields plus user_id (personalization starts here), generatedBy, readingTimeMin, counts, thread, threadFaithfulness, and per item why · example · connection · ninety · faithfulness, plus _enforcements listing anything code stripped.

data/state/usage.json
Append-only ledger: tokens and estimated cost per call. Read at the start of the next run by the circuit-breaker — this is the cost feedback loop.

data/evals/golden/<date>/
A frozen case: input.json (copy of that day’s verified file), output.json (copy of the brief), labels.json (hand-written verdicts). Copies, never references — so a re-run cannot move the baseline.

blocks.html: Two rows are deliberately both directions — gatekeeper_<date>.json (one agent’s output is the next one’s input) and usage.json (written by a run, read by the next). That is why data/ is organised by lifecycle stage rather than “input” and “output” folders.

head: Step
Where
rows: Load profile, raw day, system prompt (plain file read)
Cost circuit-breaker: month-to-date spend vs MONTHLY_BUDGET_USD; abort before spending
frame_day() — one streamed call, all items + thread, schema-enforced, prompt cached
build_check_payload() — writing first, ground truth second; headlines excluded
normalise_verdict() — verify spans are literal substrings; downgrade invented citations; derive the flag list; warn on numeric tokens that are present
assemble_day() — merge framing, enforce DO-THIS and example scope, compute reading time + counts
Write the brief; append to the usage ledger

Why

Check cap is large because the grader must enumerate claims and quote spans

In-code breaker, under the $10 workspace cap and $25 org cap

Plain meaning
Example
rows: What the news actually said. The only ground truth; lives in the Gatekeeper file
One checkable statement the grader extracted from the writing — phrased as the writing phrased it
The grader’s receipt: the exact quote from the excerpt it says backs the claim (or null)

blocks.label: Evals for the Framer — how the gate works

blocks.html: The harness answers one question: “did my last change break something that used to work?” It does that by holding the data still and re-running the current code against it.

items: The yardstick is frozen. data/evals/golden/2026-08-04/ is a copy of one past day — input, output and labels — that never changes. Today’s news flows through data/verified/ and data/briefs/ and never touches it.

What varies between runs is your system, not the data. Same seven items, same labels; only the prompt and code differ. So a red run can only have been caused by your edit — that attribution is the entire point.
It calls the real grader, not a copy: framer.check_faithfulness() is imported and invoked, so what you test is what runs. The stored verdicts in the frozen brief are historical and ignored.
It compares conclusions, not text. Labels match by pattern, so the grader may rephrase a claim freely; what must hold is the verdict.

Three checks: faithfulness (hard gate, ~$0.013) · structural assertions (hard gate, free — DO-THIS scope, example scope, sources, thread, counts recomputed with the Framer’s own functions) · usefulness rubric (soft, ~$0.006).
The output is an exit code. Non-zero blocks the change. A gate that cannot fail is not a gate — which is why the harness is itself tested by deliberately corrupting a copy and confirming it goes red.
Labels grow, never mutate. Every new bug becomes a permanent case; editing an old label to make a red test green deletes your own safety net.

blocks.html: Known gaps, all queued for Phase 6: the harness regrades the frozen brief, so a change to the Framer’s prompt is never exercised (needs a regenerate mode); flagged claims are surfaced but not regenerated (needs a bounded retry); and the free structural checks don’t run on live days (needs a daily smoke test). Also: every golden unit currently has expected_unsupported: [], so the missed-hallucination path is exercised only by manual negative tests, not automatically.

Discovers and ingests candidate items across the interest graph. In: config/scout-sources.md (Tier A–D seed list), config/profile.json. Process: fetch — likely via MCP servers for web/arXiv/GitHub — deduplicate, tag each item with its source and tier. Out: a raw candidate pool for the Gatekeeper. Graded on: recall — of what mattered, how much did it fetch. Its hard problem is that misses are invisible without an independent oracle.

Kills noise. In: Scout’s candidate pool. Process: provenance → corroboration (single-source rumour is held) → novelty dedup → reputation priors → materiality against the profile; everything killed is logged to the Suppressed drawer. Out: data/verified/gatekeeper_<date>.json — the contract the Framer consumes. Graded on: precision and recall, deliberately biased toward recall, because a false negative here is FOMO. Also owns the volume guard that protects the Framer’s single-call design.

Turns the week into practice. In: the week’s briefs + your GitHub repos. Process: pick one or two coherent concepts, design a 60-minute exercise (setup excluded), ground it in a real module or propose a new repo; runs Friday evening / Saturday morning so the expensive repo reasoning is batched. Out: backlog items in data/state/backlog.json. Graded on: code-grounding (assertion-checkable — does the module it names exist?) plus behavioural signals: completion rate, actual time, later reuse. Refactor due here: lift the faithfulness grader out of framer.py into a shared module rather than copying it.

Learns your taste. In: signal/noise ratings, homework completions, and explicit “explore X” intent. Process: adjust source reputation and topic priors; assign credit backwards across a delayed pipeline; never act on n=1. Out: updated config/profile.json. Graded on: the slope of every other metric over weeks — it cannot be evaluated on a single run. Guardrails: a diversity floor against echo chambers, and no automated prompt edits — optimising to satisfy your own gate is how a system learns to write vaguer claims and pass.

The front door, and the only agent wired to a live API. In: whatever you do in the UI — a dropped URL, a question, a rating, an intent. Process: classify intent and route (URL → Scout, question → chat over the brief, feedback → Tuner), collate responses, run checks. LLM-routed with deterministic fast-paths: explicit button actions dispatch directly; only ambiguous natural language needs the model. Out: answers to you, and labelled feedback into the eval dataset.

blocks.title: Extension points — adding the next agent

items: Code in agents/<name>.py; prompt and contract as prompts/<name>-prompt.md and -contract.md.
Write output to data/<stage>/<name>_<date>.json — named for the agent that produced it.
Reuse the shared plumbing: cost breaker + usage ledger, stop-reason guard, schema-enforced output, models pinned in top-of-file constants.
Add a golden case before the agent guards anything live; hard-gate the objective axis, keep the subjective axis reported until calibrated.

blocks.html: The techniques this system is built from, and where each one actually lands in the code. Applied means it is running and the named symbol exists; designed means it is specified and not yet written. Every claim below is checkable against the repository.

These concepts are deliberately project-agnostic — they accumulate across everything I build, so the long-form write-ups (one-liner, everyday analogy, diagram, worked code) live in a separate concepts reference rather than inside this repo. This section is the index of which ones this particular system uses, and where.
Eleven techniques. Each names the symbol that implements it, so the claim is checkable against the repository rather than taken on trust.

What it is. Deterministic scaffolding built around a probabilistic model — feeding it, constraining its output, checking it, handling failure — so an unpredictable component produces dependable results.

How it lands here. The output shape is enforced at the API boundary, and a truncated or refused response exits without writing anything rather than leaving a half-built brief that renders fine. FRAMING_SCHEMA, structured_text().
What it is. A JSON schema declared at the call itself, so the model can only emit text that fits the shape you asked for.

How it lands here. No prose is ever parsed and no field is silently renamed; additionalProperties: false stops helpful invention. A required field may be null but never absent, so a missing value is a signal rather than a KeyError. output_config.
What it is. Sending N items in one request rather than N requests.

How it lands here. Cheaper, but mainly a capability requirement: the day's thread draws a line between items, and only something seeing every item at once can write it. Seven separate calls could not produce it. frame_day().
What it is. Caching the fixed prefix of a prompt so repeat calls pay a fraction for it. Stable content must precede volatile content for the prefix to match.

How it lands here. The system prompt is cached; only the changing news is re-charged. Little benefit on a once-daily run, real benefit for the chat surface where calls cluster. cache_control: ephemeral.
What it is. Sending each step to the cheapest model that can do it, rather than the best model to everything.
How it lands here. A large model writes, a small one audits. Beyond cost, a second pair of eyes beats a bigger model marking its own homework. FRAMER_MODEL Opus, CHECK_MODEL Haiku.
What it is. A spend limit enforced before work starts rather than reconciled after it.

How it lands here. Month-to-date spend is read from an append-only ledger and checked against the budget pre-flight. A feedback loop across invocations, mediated by a file. MONTHLY_BUDGET_USD, month_to_date_spend().
What it is. Splitting evaluation into what is objectively checkable — which may block a release — and what is subjective, which is reported only.

How it lands here. Factual grounding and structural rules can fail a run; the quality rubric is printed and ignored. Gating on a metric you do not yet trust teaches you to ignore gates. hard_failures → non-zero exit.
What it is. When a model checks another model, the checker is unreliable too — so its evidence must be validated by deterministic code.

How it lands here. The auditor must quote the words supporting each claim, and code confirms that quote is a literal substring of the source. A model can invent a citation; a substring match cannot be talked into agreeing. normalise_verdict(), span_found.
What it is. A check that returns different answers on identical input cannot gate anything.

How it lands here. The judge samples at zero. At default sampling it disagreed with itself roughly one run in three, which would have failed builds at random and trained me to ignore the gate. The writer keeps sampling; the judge does not. temperature=0.
What it is. A small frozen set of inputs with hand-written correct answers, re-run on every change to catch what quietly breaks.

How it lands here. One real day, frozen as copies rather than references so a re-run cannot move its own baseline. It grows by accretion — each bug found becomes a permanent case that can never silently return. data/evals/golden/<date>/.
What it is. Two different checker failures needing two different defences: inventing evidence, versus staying silent about a claim.

How it lands here. Invented evidence is caught by code on every run. A skipped claim offers nothing to inspect, so it is caught only by planting a known fabrication and asserting it gets flagged — the first version of this grader passed a brief seeded with a fake valuation. check_regression().
Eight more, specified in enough detail to build, each with the phase it arrives in. Kept separate so the gap between designed and running stays visible rather than blurring.
What it is. Feedback cycles built into the system — act, observe, adjust, repeat — with a termination condition, so it self-corrects without a human in the loop.

How it lands here. Today's only loop is a regulator: the cost breaker holds a value in bounds but converges on nothing. The reflection loop that regenerates a flagged item and re-checks it is what turns "flagged" into "fixed". Bounded at one retry — a second failure is the prompt, not luck. Phase 6.
What it is. Separating an agent from its tools across a defined protocol boundary, so either side can change independently.
How it lands here. Applied where a real boundary exists: the Scout fetching from the open web, the Coach reading repositories. Not used where a plain function call would do. Phases 4 and 8.
What it is. Precision asks how much of what you flagged deserved it; recall asks how much of what deserved flagging you caught. Which you favour is a product decision, not a technical one.

How it lands here. The Gatekeeper deliberately errs toward letting things through: a false negative here is the FOMO this system exists to kill, and unlike a false positive it is invisible. Everything killed is logged so misses stay auditable. Phase 5.
What it is. Checking whether the work you are about to recommend has already been done.

How it lands here. Same repo access as code-grounding, opposite question: grounding asks whether the target exists, reconciliation asks whether the answer already does. Recall-biased — when unsure, offer the exercise with a note rather than suppress it. Phase 8.
What it is. Behaviour is stronger evidence of value than a rating, because people call things interesting that they never act on.

How it lands here. Finishing an exercise cost an hour; rating an article cost nothing. The skip reason makes it actionable — "wrong topic" corrects the Framer, "too big" corrects the Coach. Completion stays a diagnostic and never an optimisation target, or the Coach learns to write trivial exercises. Phases 7 and 10.
What it is. Attributing an outcome backwards across a delayed, multi-step pipeline to the step actually responsible.

How it lands here. A poorly rated item could be the Scout's fault for fetching it, the Gatekeeper's for passing it, or the Framer's for framing it badly. Without attribution the Tuner adjusts the wrong agent. Phase 10.
What it is. A floor on exploration that stops a personalisation loop collapsing into what you already believe.

How it lands here. The Tuner can raise my ratings by feeding me only what I agree with — scoring well while making the product worse. A standing diversity minimum prevents optimising into a filter bubble. Phase 10.
What it is. Deterministic interception points around agent execution, for policy enforcement and observability.
How it lands here. Listed because it is the obvious home for spend limits and audit logging once more than one agent runs. Not scheduled.

The through-line. Almost every concept above is a variation on one idea: the guarantee has to come from deterministic code outside the probabilistic system. The schema constrains the shape, the guard catches the truncation, the substring check proves the citation, the frozen labels catch the drift, and zero temperature stops the judge changing its mind. The model supplies judgement; the code supplies certainty. Every place that boundary blurred is a place something broke.

sections.title: Evals — how we know it works

blocks.html: Every agent is measured, component-wise and end-to-end. The recurring split: objective checks (fixed gates, automatable) vs subjective checks (personal, learned targets).

head: Agent
What we measure
Type
rows: Recall — of what mattered, how much did it fetch? (invisible-miss problem → retrospective oracle)
Precision & recall (classifier). Biased toward recall — false negatives = FOMO

Faithfulness (claim ledger → each claim carries a verbatim excerpt span; per-item vs own excerpt, thread vs the union; hard zero-hallucination gate) + Structural assertions (deterministic, no API) + Usefulness (rubric ratings, reported not gated until calibrated). The grader is itself under test against hand labels — see data/evals/
Code-grounding (assertions on your repo) + doability/skill (completion, actual time, reuse)
Slope of every other metric over time (meta-eval). Graded on trend, not level

blocks.html: Two grading modes: offline regression against a golden set of labeled past days (makes prompt iteration safe), and online production feedback (your ratings + a dashboard). The offline half is live as of Phase 3 — python data/evals/run_evals.py, exit code gates.

Who checks the checker. A grader is an agent too, and it fails the same ways. So it gets the same treatment: hand labels are the ground truth, the grader's verdicts are the prediction, and the harness reports its false positives and false negatives explicitly. Three habits fell out of finding two real false positives in our own graded output — make it show its work (enumerate every claim with a quoted span before judging), verify the evidence in code (a quoted span must literally appear in the excerpt), and give each unit only the ground truth it is entitled to (own excerpt for an item, the union for a thread that synthesizes across the day).

Measurement and fixing are kept separate. The Evaluator is a read-only sensor; the Prescriber turns diagnoses into recommended actions; the Tuner is the actuator that recalibrates agents; the Control Room reports and asks you questions, whose answers become new gold labels.

blocks.caption: Measurement, prescription and actuation are kept in separate boxes, and your answers to the Control Room become new gold labels.

blocks.html: The Tuner could raise your ratings by only feeding you what you already believe — a filter bubble that betrays the goal of balancing your thinking with new thinking. A standing diversity / exploration metric in the Control Room prevents this: a minimum share of items must sit outside your established priors.

Every recommended action records a predicted impact with a confidence. After it ships, the Control Room shows predicted vs. actual — so the prescriptive layer earns trust instead of just asserting it, and every recalibration is regression-tested against the held-out set before shipping and is reversible.

Data is separated from presentation. Agents write JSON to data/; the pages (Signal.html, Control-Hub.html) render it. Files: profile.json (the user profile), YYYY-MM-DD.json (immutable daily brief record + archive), backlog.json, metrics.json. Every record carries user_id.
Loop / token engineering: the daily path is cheap (small models for Scout/dedup, mid for Framer); the expensive repo-grounded synthesis (Coach) runs only Friday night / Saturday morning.

items: Recall over precision at the Gatekeeper — better a little noise than a missed item (FOMO).
Depth over coverage in homework — one or two coherent exercises, the rest benched to the backlog.
Faithfulness is a hard gate; usefulness is a soft, learned target.
Build for one, don't hardcode one — profile object + user_id seam keep the multi-tenant path open at near-zero cost today.

blocks.html: The brain transfers; the body doesn't. Agent logic is ~80% portable to a product; the local/single-user scaffolding is not. Key economics insight: most of the pipeline is shared — the news is the same for everyone, so run Scout → Gatekeeper once to produce a canonical verified pool, then apply a cheap per-user personalization layer (Framer framing + materiality + Coach) on top. What a product adds: auth + multi-tenant isolation, per-user LLM cost management, per-user cold-start onboarding, and cloud scheduling. Defensibility is the action loop (news → hands-on skill grounded in the user's code) and adaptive personalization — not the news itself.

Treat the system as an experiment: hypotheses (each agent's value), metrics (the evals above), controlled iteration (offline regression before shipping any prompt change), and honest reporting of predicted vs. actual. The append-only Decision Log below is the lab notebook.

decisionLog.lead: Practice is the system's revealed-preference loop, and completion rate must never be a target.
decisionLog.body: The signals existed scattered across the spec but the circuit was never described. Naming it: brief item → exercise → I finish, skip or overrun → the Tuner reads the behaviour → tomorrow's brief changes. The asymmetry is the point. A rating on a brief item is stated preference and is weak evidence — people call things interesting they never act on. Finishing an exercise is revealed preference: it cost an hour, and it is the only place this system obtains that class of signal. The skip reason is what makes it actionable — "wrong topic" corrects the Framer's priors, "too big" corrects the Coach's scoping, and without distinguishing them a skip is uninterpretable. New guardrail: if the Tuner optimises completion rate, the Coach learns to generate trivial exercises — completion rises, the product degrades, and the metric reports success throughout. Completion is therefore a diagnostic read only alongside actual-vs-estimated time and code reuse, never an optimisation target. Recorded in metrics.json beside the diversity guardrail. Also: the prior-art verdict is itself gateable — it is answerable against the repo — so it joins code-grounding on the objective axis rather than being taken on trust.

decisionLog.lead: Coach must reconcile against my repos before offering an exercise, not only ground in them.
decisionLog.body: Phase 8 already gives the Coach repo access to verify that the module an exercise targets exists — grounding. The same access answers the opposite question, which was never specified: have I already built this? Assigning an hour of work that is finished in a repo is the fastest way for a recommender to lose trust, and no amount of good writing survives it. Three states: none offers as written, partial narrows the exercise to start from what exists, built retires it and returns a pointer to the code. Recall-biased on purpose, matching the Gatekeeper: a wrong already built silently withholds an exercise I never learn existed — invisible, and precisely the failure mode this system exists to prevent — while a wrong no prior art costs a few minutes and corrects itself the moment I open the repo. When unsure, offer with a note; never suppress.

decisionLog.lead: Repo made public, with the private surface reframed rather than removed.
decisionLog.body: Audited first: .env was never committed and no key literal appears anywhere in history — every blob scanned, not just the current tree, so nothing irreversible was at stake. Two judgement calls followed. profile.json was rewritten as a statement of the reader problem rather than a personal bio — it always was the personalization seam, and framing it that way is both more honest about its role and removes a career-intent line that had no business being public. Control-Hub was kept rather than stripped: its badge and footer read "never publish", which a published page cannot carry, so both were reworded to "private surface · sample data". The surface is still the private one in the design — this instance is publishable only because its numbers are placeholders. Stripping the files would have needed a history rewrite, and the commit history is itself the artifact worth showing. Added an MIT licence, and GitHub Pages so the four HTML surfaces render instead of showing 800KB of bundle source; all seven cross-links between them verified to resolve.

decisionLog.lead: Content/design split adopted for every document — with two classes.
decisionLog.body: All pages become JSON content + a design produced in Claude Design; the JSON is the source of truth and the HTML is never hand-edited. But the two classes need different deliverables. Static docs (Concepts, Plan, System-Design) carry content I maintain, change weekly, and can be regenerated on demand — a finished page is fine. Live surfaces (Signal.html, Control-Hub.html) render agent output that changes daily, so regeneration is impossible: Claude Design must deliver a renderer with a data slot, and the design has to be locked before Phase 6 so the backend can be wired into a fixed template. Locking means freezing the data contract the template reads, not just the visuals. First working example of the pattern: the Knowledge Hub (Agentic_Concepts.json → generated page).

decisionLog.lead: Low-level architecture restructured per agent.
decisionLog.body: One subsection each for Framer (built, in depth) and Scout · Gatekeeper · Coach · Tuner · Orchestrator (designed, one paragraph each: in / process / out / graded on). The Framer's dense internals diagram was replaced with a three-tile inputs → process → outputs flow after it proved hard to read. Module map reordered input → process → output, with the data-contract shapes folded into the path descriptions rather than living in a separate section. Added a side-by-side faithfulness vs usefulness comparison, a terminology table with worked examples (claim, supporting_span, expected_span_contains, false alarm, missed hallucination, omission, grader error, precision, recall), and a plain-language "how the Framer eval gate works" subsection capturing the walkthrough — frozen yardstick, same-function-not-a-copy, conclusions-not-text, and the four known gaps.

decisionLog.lead: Deterministic false-alarm signal added to the grader.
decisionLog.body: When a claim is marked unsupported with no span, Python now scans the claim for numeric tokens (money, percentages, dates) and warns if they appear verbatim in the excerpt — the $965B case, catchable for free. It warns, never promotes: a number's presence says nothing about the claim built on it ("$122B" is in the excerpt; "SoftBank invested $122B" is still false). Proper nouns were dropped from the check — every claim names its own subject, so they fired on fabrications too. This is the only false-alarm signal code can produce: verifying evidence is present is mechanical; verifying it is absent is a semantic judgement Python cannot make.

decisionLog.lead: Three gaps found by walking the design, all deferred to Phase 6.
decisionLog.body: (1) Flagged ≠ fixed — the Framer's faithfulness check surfaces unsupported claims but writes the brief anyway; the reflection loop is one turn, not a retry. (2) No daily check — run_evals.py only runs against frozen golden cases when something changes, so a contract violation on a live day goes unnoticed until the next prompt edit; the free structural checks should run daily as a smoke test. (3) The harness regression-tests the grader, not the writer — it regrades the frozen brief, so a change to the Framer's own prompt is never exercised. Closing that needs an opt-in "regenerate mode" that re-runs the Framer on the golden input before grading (costs one Opus call).

decisionLog.lead: Batching is a default, not a hard requirement — corrected.
decisionLog.body: Framing all items in one call makes cross-item connections free, but a multi-call design is viable: chunk the items, then add an explicit reduce call to write the thread (N+1 calls), accepting weaker per-item connections across chunk boundaries. The real ceiling is output tokens (~60–70 items at the current 24k cap), not context. No dynamic chunking is built, and it may never be needed: the Gatekeeper is supposed to cap volume — a 60-item day means the Gatekeeper failed, not that the Framer needs sharding. Action for Phase 5: add a loud assertion on item count rather than silently truncating.

decisionLog.lead: Added a Low-level architecture section.
decisionLog.body: The page had the architectural why but no implementation depth, so detail lived only in code and commit messages. Now captured: module map with BUILT / DESIGNED status tags, the Framer's 8-step execution order (2 API calls, everything else deterministic), model-routing and cost knobs with observed spend, the raw→framed data contract, grader internals, eval harness structure, and extension points for the next agent. Living section — updated as each agent lands.

decisionLog.lead: Prompt and contract split into separate files.
decisionLog.body: prompts/framer-prompt.md now holds the system prompt and nothing else; prompts/framer-contract.md holds the I/O contract and hard rules. The tell was the marker-extraction regex in framer.py — machinery that existed only to separate two things sharing one file; the loader is now a plain read. Rationale: a prompt-only change shows as a prompt-only diff, and future voice variants map cleanly as N prompt files against one shared contract instead of N duplicated copies. Drift is managed by discipline (change both in the same commit) and by the structural assertions, which already test the contract's rules. Pattern generalises: each agent gets <agent>-prompt.md + <agent>-contract.md in prompts/.

decisionLog.lead: Known limit, carried forward.
decisionLog.body: The gate is deterministic for a fixed input, which is what regression needs, but on unseen days the Haiku grader still occasionally enumerates an inference ("X means Y no longer matters") as a checkable claim. Acceptable while the golden day is fixed; revisit before the grader guards live briefs — most likely by routing it to a stronger model, which is also what the usefulness judge needs before it can gate.

decisionLog.lead: Golden set: frozen copies, and labels that admit uncertainty.
decisionLog.body: data/evals/golden/<date>/ holds input.json + output.json as frozen copies — evaluating the live files would let a Framer re-run silently move the baseline. Labels carry three tiers per unit: expected_unsupported (must flag), tolerated (genuinely borderline under the Framer's own contract — scored neither way, deliberately kept short), and named regression_cases asserted against the claim ledger rather than merely the flag list, so we can demand the grader looked at the $965B clause and found the span. Adding a day is a new directory; the runner globs and needs no edit. A second false positive surfaced during labelling — the 2026-08-13 re-run flagged "~80% of Q1 dollars", which its excerpt states word for word — and is seeded as the second regression case.

decisionLog.lead: Verify the verifier's evidence, in code.
decisionLog.body: Every span the grader quotes is checked as a literal substring of the excerpt; a claim "supported" by a span that isn't there is downgraded to unsupported and recorded as a grader error, gated separately from false positives. A grader can invent a citation; a substring match cannot. Paired with temperature=0 on the grader — at default sampling it disagreed with itself on borderline sentences roughly one run in three, which would have failed builds at random (5/5 clean runs after; fabrication detection unaffected).

decisionLog.lead: Root cause of the $965B false positive: grading scope, not carelessness.
decisionLog.body: The grader was handed source_excerpt first and the framing second, and so enumerated the excerpt's claims and checked them against the excerpt — grading the ground truth against itself. It never read the framing, which is why a supported claim looked unsupported and, as a seeded fabrication test proved, why invented facts passed clean. Fixes: the writing under test comes first in the payload and is named writing_under_test; the excerpt is named ground_truth_excerpt; each claim must be phrased as the writing phrases it and carry a verbatim supporting span before any verdict; headlines are excluded (the Gatekeeper wrote them); and the day-level thread is graded against the union of every excerpt, never one item's. Flag lists are now derived in code from the claim ledger rather than taken as a second free-text field.

decisionLog.lead: Phase 3 done (Opus 5). The Framer grader is now itself under test.
decisionLog.body: data/evals/run_evals.py runs three checks over each frozen golden day: faithfulness (hard gate, one Haiku call — regrades the committed framing and compares to hand labels, reporting false positives and false negatives), structural assertions (hard gate, no API — DO THIS only on AI, worked examples only on allowed categories, sources present, thread non-empty, reading time and counts recomputed with the Framer's own functions), and usefulness (LLM judge on a four-part rubric, printed but not gating until calibrated against real ratings). Non-zero exit gates future prompt changes. ~$0.02 per run, on the same ledger and circuit-breaker as the Framer.

decisionLog.lead: Repo reorganised by role; data named by producing agent.
decisionLog.body: Flat root replaced with agents/ · application/ · config/ · data/ · design/ · plan/ · prompts/. Three principles: (1) config vs data — hand-authored files that rarely change (profile.json, scout-sources.md) live in config/, machine-generated files in data/; (2) no input/output folders — the same file is one agent's output and the next agent's input, so data/ splits by lifecycle (verified/ · briefs/ · state/ · evals/) and each file is prefixed with the agent that wrote it (gatekeeper_YYYY-MM-DD.json → framer_YYYY-MM-DD.json); (3) telemetry is its own tier (data/state/). Retired News-reference.html — application/Signal.html now renders that design live, so the p2 prompt points there instead. All hardcoded paths in agents/framer.py, every doc/prompt reference, and all cross-page links were updated and verified.

decisionLog.lead: Visual design system adopted.
decisionLog.body: All surfaces now share one theme: warm cream #f2ebdc page, #faf5ea cards, rust-terracotta #b5502a accent, forest green #2f6b52 for positive/DO THIS, Newsreader serif headlines + Public Sans body. Applied to Signal, System-Design, Plan, Control-Hub, and the Knowledge Hub concepts reference. Architecture diagrams stay on dark cards for legibility on the light page.

decisionLog.lead: Surfaces split by lifecycle.
decisionLog.body: The combined Signal page became two single-purpose files: Signal.html (the daily News brief — regenerated by the Framer) and System-Design.html (this living design record — hand-updated each session). Rationale: the two have different update rhythms, and a compiled/bundled design page can't be hand-edited, which broke the decision-log ritual. Both stay editable plain HTML so the design and maintainability coexist. Cross-references updated in CONVENTIONS.md, Plan.html, README, and the Framer docs.

decisionLog.lead: New agent: Orchestrator (front door).
decisionLog.body: Merges the original Interactive + Feedback agents. Sits between the UI and the agents: classifies user intent, routes (add-source → Scout, question → chat, feedback / "explore X" → Tuner), collates responses, runs checks, surfaces results. LLM-routed with deterministic fast-paths — explicit UI actions dispatch directly; the LLM handles only ambiguous natural-language input. It's the single live-API agent in front of the otherwise-batch pipeline (this bounds the hosting/backend work). Lands ~Phase 9; its v0 is the chatbot.

decisionLog.lead: Infrastructure trajectory.
decisionLog.body: Data: JSON files now → SQLite when history/queries get awkward (~Phase 6–9) → Postgres + pgvector (incl. auth sessions) at multi-tenant (Phase 11); the user_id seam keeps the migration mechanical. Observability: extend usage.json into a structured per-run trace now → an LLM-observability tool at deploy (~Phase 6+); it overlaps the eval subsystem and feeds the Control Room. Cost tracker: the usage.json ledger + cost circuit-breaker exist now; the Control Room charts it live in Phase 9.

decisionLog.lead: Process.
decisionLog.body: Decisions are now recorded in both Plan.html and this Decision Log (see prompts/CONVENTIONS.md §5).

decisionLog.lead: Tool layer & decoupling.
decisionLog.body: Agents are decoupled from each other via JSON contracts, and from their tools via MCP where a real boundary exists (Scout fetching, Coach GitHub). Captured as the per-agent concept map above rather than a one-line entry.

decisionLog.lead: Eval finding.
decisionLog.body: The faithfulness check produced a false positive (missed a clause; graded the thread against a single item's excerpt). Decision: the grader needs its own eval, and the thread is checked against the union of all excerpts — Phase 3's first golden-set case.

decisionLog.lead: Phase 2 done (commit df8adfd, Opus 5).
